```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(knbsdata)
```

The Statistical Abstract is KNBS's annual compendium, and since the 2025
edition its chapter tables ship as Excel workbooks on the KNBS website —
eighteen chapters from Land & Water to Social & Economic Inclusion.
`knbs_publications()` finds those workbooks and
`knbs_download_publication()` fetches them verified; this vignette is about
the step beyond: reading a table *inside* a workbook as clean tidy
observations.

## Curated, not guessed

A published spreadsheet is a print layout, not a dataset: title rows, merged
headers, section headings, footnote lines, dot leaders, provisional marks.
A universal spreadsheet-to-tidy converter would have to guess its way
through all of that, and a wrong guess produces plausible, wrong data — the
worst outcome this package knows.

So extraction here is **curated**. Each supported table has a hand-verified
recipe in the package's registry: which sheet, which title anchor, which
rows are section headings, what the unit is, and several reference values
read from the workbook by hand at curation time. Every extraction re-checks
all of it. If KNBS reshuffles a sheet or revises a pinned figure, you get
`knbs_error_schema_changed` or `knbs_error_validation_failed` with an
explanation — never silently re-arranged numbers.

Curated so far: **Chapter 2, National Accounts** — fifteen tables covering
the production accounts, GDP by activity at current and constant prices,
expenditure on GDP, capital formation, national income, and saving. The
registry is the extension point for further chapters.

## Listing and fetching

```{r}
knbs_abstract_tables()
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
gdp <- knbs_abstract_table("2.2")     # GDP by activity, current prices
gdp[gdp$industry == "GDP at market prices", c("period", "status", "value")]
#> # A tibble: 10 x 3
#>    period status         value
#>     <int> <chr>          <dbl>
#>  1   2015 NA           6884326
#>  2   2016 NA           7594064
#>  ...
#>  9   2023 revised     15033610
#> 10   2024 provisional 16224478
```

A table id works, and so does enough of a title:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
saving <- knbs_abstract_table("disposable income")   # resolves to 2.9
```

## Reading the columns

- `period` is the integer year, and `status` carries the source's own year
  flags: `"provisional"` (printed `*`), `"revised"` (printed `+`), `NA` for
  final years.
- The row dimension keeps its meaning as a named column: `industry` for the
  GDP tables, `expenditure_category`, `purpose` for capital formation.
- Sectioned tables carry their section as a second named column. In the
  production accounts (`"2.1"`), `industry` is the section and `measure`
  the row — output, intermediate consumption, value added, compensation.
- A row the source prints without figures — "Less: Subsidies" in the
  production accounts — is kept with `NA` values, because that is what the
  source shows.
- Units are stated in `knbs_metadata()`, not repeated on every row; a
  mixed-unit table (2.8 carries KSh million aggregates *and* per-capita
  KSh) says so there.

## Into the tidyverse

Every result is a tibble, so dplyr verbs work directly — and they keep the
provenance: filter it, rank it, transform it, and `knbs_metadata()` still
answers on the result. Aggregations and reshapes return plain tibbles,
because a derived table is your data, not the source's.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# The largest industries in 2024, straight off the table
knbs_abstract_table("2.2") |>
  filter(period == 2024, industry != "GDP at market prices") |>
  slice_max(value, n = 5) |>
  select(industry, value, status)

# Recreate the printed-table look: industries by year, wide
knbs_abstract_table("2.4") |>
  filter(industry %in% c("Agriculture, forestry and fishing",
                         "Manufacturing", "GDP at market prices")) |>
  select(industry, period, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = value)

# Sectioned tables group naturally
knbs_abstract_table("2.1") |>
  filter(measure == "Gross value added at basic prices", period == 2024) |>
  arrange(desc(value))

# And straight into ggplot2
library(ggplot2)
knbs_abstract_table("2.5") |>
  filter(industry == "GDP at market prices") |>
  ggplot(aes(period, value)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Real GDP growth", y = "per cent")
```

To hand the data to something that dislikes subclasses, drop the wrapper
with `tibble::as_tibble()`.

## Provenance travels

```{r, eval = FALSE}
meta <- knbs_metadata(gdp)
meta$source_url   # the workbook on knbs.or.ke
meta$notes        # edition, sheet, workbook SHA-256, flag legend
knbs_cite(gdp)
```

The workbook itself is downloaded once through the package's verify layer —
an HTML page arriving where a spreadsheet was expected is refused — cached
locally, and hashed; the SHA-256 in the notes says exactly which file the
numbers came from.

## What this is not

- **Not a universal parser.** Only curated tables extract; everything else
  in the workbooks remains available as verified downloads through
  `knbs_download_publication()`.
- **Not a modelling of the tables' arithmetic.** Aggregate rows ("GDP at
  market prices", "Total") are rows like any other, as printed; nothing is
  summed, derived or reconciled for you.
- **Not immune to source revisions — by design.** A changed workbook stops
  extraction until the registry is re-verified against it. That is the
  honest failure mode.
